newsitem.title: CHINA: China says needs patriotic action to build power.
newsitem.headline: China says needs patriotic action to build power.

text.p: Chinese consumers should buy Chinese goods and businessmen must be wary of their overseas partners if China is to turn patriotic cant into action and become a strong nation commanding respect, official media said.

Building national power was essential in a world where foreign politicians put their own nations first and international investors saw profit as the bottom line, the Outlook magazine said in an edition available on Thursday.

"Strength is the basis of foreign relations. Without strength, everything else is out of the question," Outlook said in a signed editorial, the latest in a series of official nationalist exhortations issued by China's state media.
"When China becomes strong, nobody in the world will dare to bully us," said the magazine, which is published by Beijing's official mouthpiece, the Xinhua news agency said.

A gale of officially sponsored nationalism has swept China in recent months, fuelled by calls for more patriotism and state media denunciations of Western nations judged to be interfering in China's internal affairs or insulting its honour.
Analysts say Beijing is using nationalism to try to fill the ideological gap left in the nation's psyche as rapid economic reforms make traditional Marxism increasingly irrelevant.

A widening dispute with Japan over an island group in the East China Sea and recent U.S "gunboat policy" in the Taiwan Strait had been an education for the Chinese people, who should now soberly consider how to love their country, Outlook said.

Disagreement between Beijing and Tokyo over ownership of the islands, known in Chinese as the Diaoyus and in Japanese as the Senkakus, resurfaced in July after Japanese rightists built a lighthouse on one of the islands.

The row came just months after a major chill in Sino-U.S. ties in March, when Beijing carried out intimidatory missile tests and military exercises in waters off arch-rival Taiwan in the run-up to the island's first direct presidential elections.
Washington responded by sending two aircraft carrier battlegroups to the seas nearby, infuriating Beijing.
Outlook said true patriotism meant change was needed to curb over-enthusiasm for foreign brands and the willingness of some Chinese to sacrifice national interests in their dealings with foreigners.
Chinese consumers were so much in love with overseas brands that they rushed to buy them even if the product was made in China, it said.
"If you just stick on an overseas label, people flock to it like ducks -- and even if they clearly understand that it is a fake foreign brand, they still feel good wearing it," it said.
While campaigns to boycott imports from individual nations would not be appropriate, China should learn from the example of South Koreans and favour domestically produced goods.
Vigilance was needed to guard China's interests in business dealings with the outside world, said Outlook.
Chinese should not be credulous when overseas firms claimed they wanted to help the nation's modernisation or when foreign politicians said they hoped for a strong and prosperous China.
"Normally, capitalists are concerned with profit, while politicians are concerned with the national interests of their own nations," the magazine said.

It was impossible to know how much wealth and resources had been lost to the depredations of foreign businesses by officials desperate to attract foreign investments, it said, adding it was not enough to merely talk of love for the nation.
"Patriotism is not empty words...patriotism is real actions," it said.
